title: Politics should be more boring
gist: Yglesias argues that the electoral value of being an exciting, attention-commanding politician is confined almost entirely to primaries; boringness is irrelevant to winning general elections and to governing well, so a nomination process that penalizes dull-but-effective candidates like Andy Beshear or Roy Cooper is broken.

insights.claim: The penalty for being a boring politician applies almost entirely to primaries, not general elections, because primary electorates differ fundamentally from general electorates.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Separates a candidate's viral appeal (a primary asset) from general-election electability, warning against reading nomination-stage buzz as a signal of November strength.
insights.quote: when we say that “boring” is a handicap for a politician, we’re really just talking about primaries
insights.locator: A primary problem, not a general-election one

insights.claim: Commanding attention is critical in primaries because candidates are poorly distinguished from each other in the eyes of normal voters, so already-famous or viral candidates hold a real advantage.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains why fame (Biden 2020, Cuomo in the NYC mayoral primary) outperforms in crowded primaries but decays in general elections where both sides get heavy coverage.
insights.quote: while the ability to command attention always has some value in politics, it’s critical in a primary
insights.locator: In particular, while the ability to command attention

insights.claim: David Crowley needed heavy help from Governor Tony Evers to become known enough to beat Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, yet is now up in the polls, favored in Nate Silver's model, and ahead in betting odds.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete case that a candidate's struggle to stand out in a primary carries essentially no implication for general-election competitiveness.
insights.quote: Crowley is currently up in the polls, favored in Nate Silver’s model, and way ahead in the betting odds.
insights.locator: David Crowley eventually beat Francesca Hong

insights.claim: The pivotal swing voter has shifted from the complacent, content 1990s type who thought Clinton was fine to today's “double-haters” who dislike both nominees.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes modern campaigns as a contest to win voters who reject both candidates, a very different targeting problem than persuading satisfied moderates.
insights.quote: In every recent election, the key swing vote has been “double-haters”

insights.claim: In October 1996 Bill Clinton had a 54 percent job-approval rating but won only 49 percent of the vote, illustrating a lower-stakes political era where satisfied voters might still defect.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A benchmark for how much the approval-to-vote relationship has tightened; today's polarized electorate converts approval into votes far more directly.
insights.quote: in October of 1996, Clinton had a 54 percent job approval rating but only got 49 percent of the vote

insights.claim: Many low-key, even dull governors win consistently — Laura Kelly, Andy Beshear, Katie Hobbs, Josh Stein, and Tony Evers among Democrats, Phil Scott and Kelly Ayotte among Republicans.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Evidence that general-election success does not require charisma, undercutting the media premium on viral, attention-commanding candidates.
insights.locator: there are lots of politically successful governors

insights.claim: Boring former Governor Roy Cooper is cruising to a Senate win in North Carolina, yet the media produced roughly 100 times as many articles on what Democrats can learn from Zohran Mamdani as from Cooper.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Media attention tracks who commands attention, not who is most electorally instructive — so the loudest 'lessons' can be the least relevant to actually beating Republicans.
insights.quote: we’ve had about 100 times as many articles asking what lessons Democrats can learn from Mamdani as articles asking what they can learn from Cooper
insights.locator: We also know that boring former Governor Roy Cooper

insights.claim: Mastering the attention economy is not actually all that important to political success; a candidate who avoids a contested primary can be a formidable general-election nominee without being viral.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A directly against-consensus claim in a media environment that treats virality as the key skill; implies undervalued 'boring' candidates are systematically overlooked.
insights.quote: the lesson we should learn from Cooper is that mastering the attention economy isn’t actually all that important

insights.claim: Split Ticket's table of 2024 races decided by candidate quality flagged Kristen McDonald Rivet — an obscure figure who is not a viral star or in-demand podcast guest — as a stellar electoral performer.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Points to quantitative candidate-quality metrics as a better guide to electoral strength than media prominence.
insights.locator: When I first saw this Split Ticket table

insights.claim: 'Exciting' can become a stand-in for appealing to one's own social peers, so media figures who find Mamdani more exciting than McDonald Rivet may just be reflecting their Brooklyn-centric social world.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A caution that pundit excitement is a biased proxy; broad-electorate appeal often looks unglamorous to coastal-media tastes.
insights.quote: “exciting” can easily become a stand-in for the idea of appealing to our specific social peers
insights.locator: I think all of us who work in the media

themes.theme: The electorate is not the media

insights.claim: Most American voters are over 50, live in the suburbs of mid-sized metro areas, and lack college degrees.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A demographic reality check for anyone calibrating messaging to online or coastal-elite tastes rather than the median voter.
insights.quote: Most voters are over 50 years old, live in the suburbs of mid-sized metro areas, and don’t have college degrees.
insights.locator: But this is a big country

insights.claim: Obama's underdog 2008 primary win was powered by upscale 'wine track' liberals and working-class African Americans, but his 2012 re-election was secured by non-college white Midwesterners he spent enormous effort courting.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows the primary-winning and general-winning coalitions can be different groups, reinforcing that primary strength does not equal general strength.
insights.locator: Obama was beloved by “wine track” upscale liberals

insights.claim: Addressing prices, affordability, and cost of living hinges on tedious technical issues most voters are not inclined to study, so the exciting parts of politics are not the parts central to governing.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Implies leaders selected for charisma may be poorly matched to the wonky work of actually improving affordability outcomes.
insights.quote: the parts of politics that people find exciting or interesting aren’t really the parts that are central to governing

insights.claim: Obama's economic recovery was too slow because congressional Democrats and the White House built the stimulus on an incorrect analysis of both the macroeconomic situation and the legislative dynamics.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Attributes a defining presidential shortfall to analytic error rather than politics, underscoring that competence at unglamorous analysis drives outcomes.
insights.quote: congressional Democrats had an incorrect analysis of the macroeconomic situation
insights.locator: if you look at what held Obama back

insights.claim: Biden-era immigration policy underrated the push-and-pull factors driving the asylum surge, was over-optimistic that it would subside, and reacted too slowly — its eventual actions worked but came too late.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Frames the asylum surge as a diagnosable analytic failure with a lag, useful for anticipating how administrations misjudge migration dynamics.
insights.quote: They underrated the push and pull factors that created the surge of asylum claimants
insights.locator: I’m still not entirely sure what went down

insights.claim: Presidents make destructive misjudgments even when incentivized to get things right, as with Bush's belief that invading Iraq would work out and Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A reminder that incentive alignment does not guarantee good analysis, so leadership selection should weight judgment over showmanship.
insights.locator: Presidents, unfortunately, sometimes judge the situation incorrectly

insights.claim: It is hard to imagine Andy Beshear securing a presidential nomination on a platform of managerial competence and Medicaid expansion, illustrating how the process penalizes competent-but-dull candidates.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Names a specific electorally strong figure the system likely screens out, a marker of the mismatch between nomination criteria and governing ability.
insights.quote: It’s really hard to imagine Andy Beshear securing the presidential nomination on a platform of managerial competence and Medicaid expansion.
insights.locator: A primary problem, not a general-election one

insights.claim: If being boring is a crippling handicap in the nomination process while being irrelevant to winning general elections and governing well, that is a damning indictment of the nomination process itself.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The article's core conclusion: parties select nominees on a criterion (excitement) unrelated to the two things that matter, systematically degrading candidate quality.
insights.quote: that seems like a really damning indictment of the process
